doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Taking up the electric bass and moving to studio work
summary: He bought an electric bass in 1952, then returned to it after hearing Aretha Franklin, Jerry Jemmott and Chuck Rainey, since New York recording was mostly electric.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: And your children were born, let me figure, late 70s?
Well, my daughter Carol was born in 1971, my son Michael was born in 1974.
Okay. And that’s when you started to — was your pick-up of the electric bass, no pun intended, that was about that time?
Thank you. Was that about the same time? Did that happen because you wanted to stay home more, and the electric bass became something you needed to do?

Well I never made any real courageous decisions about staying home, it was just sort of little teeny decisions. I took up the electric bass when I was twelve, in 1952. I bought a Humbucker, a Gibson Humbucker, because I was, I don’t know, somehow or other I just bought one and my brother and I were doing a little bit of fooling around with it. And it was in my guitar days, it was before I took the upright up. So I played it, and I said yeah, I can play this, and I’m sort of playing it, and then I put it away. Then I moved to New York and all of a sudden I heard Aretha Franklin and Jerry Jemmott and I guess Chuck Rainey play. I said now I like that, that’s good electric playing. I mean this is [scats]. I said, yeah, I could get into that now. So I got electric bass and I realized they were doing a lot of commercials, and the recording business was mostly on electric bass in New York, even in 1967 when I moved back to town. And I guess I just said I’ve got to buy one. I know I can play it, I know I’ve got the basics of it down. So I took a couple of gigs at night where I worked just playing electric bass, electric bass, and my upright chops went out the window but I didn’t care because nobody was calling me to play. In those days jazz had sort of taken a deep dive underground. I mean the public just lost it. Jazz got so complex and convoluted and nobody was playing swing anymore, nobody was playing simple songs that non-jazzers could understand. So the public said well forget jazz. Rock & roll, that’s what we like, rock & roll. And so what happened was is pop music started taking on the characteristics of early jazz. All of a sudden Aretha was — I mean certain areas of pop music were starting to take over where early jazz had been so communicative. To me, pop music was starting to do this. And then all of a sudden, so in the ‘70s jazz was in a very underground state. And in my opinion, the guy who caused it to turn around, now you’d never guess this, but in my opinion it was Scott Hamilton. He started playing jazz that people could relate to. And all of a sudden his music became very popular. Swing jazz. He came in sort of like Lester Young and started playing like this. And I watched this tremendous resurgence occur right around the time that he was really getting popular.
